elements.id-string-22: \textbf{Symmetry plays a key role in determining the physical properties of materials.
elements.id-string-23: By Neumann's principle, the properties of a material are invariant under the symmetry operations of the space group to which the material belongs.
elements.id-string-24: Continuous phase transitions are associated with a spontaneous reduction in symmetry.
elements.id-string-25: (For example, the onset of ferromagnetism spontaneously breaks time reversal symmetry.) Much less common are examples where proximity to a continuous phase transition leads to an increase in symmetry.
elements.id-string-26: Here, we find an emergent tetragonal symmetry close to an apparent charge density wave (CDW) bicritical point in a fundamentally orthorhombic material, ErTe$_3$, for which the CDW phase transitions are tuned via anisotropic strain.
elements.id-string-27: The underlying structure of the material remains orthorhombic for all applied strains, including at the  bicritical point, due to a glide plane symmetry in the crystal structure.
elements.id-string-28: Nevertheless, the observation of a divergence in the anisotropy of the in-plane elastoresistivity reveals an emergent electronic tetragonality near the  bicritical point.}
elements.id-string-30: ErTe$_3$, like other rare earth tritellurides (RTe$_3$), belongs to the orthorhombic space group Cmcm ($D^{17}_{2h}$, no 63).
elements.id-string-31: The structure comprises bilayers of almost square-planar Te nets, separated along the $b$-axis by RTe block layers.
elements.id-string-32: At room temperature, the $a$ and $c$ lattice parameters are almost identical, $a=0.999c$, and it is possible to tune these values using externally applied anisotropic strain, such that the material is tuned from $a>c$ to $a<c$.
elements.id-string-33: Despite this near equivalence of the in-plane lattice parameters, the presence of a glide plane between the Te bilayers (illustrated in Figure \ref{fig1}(a)) makes the material fundamentally orthorhombic.
elements.id-string-34: The glide plane operation is a non-symmorphic symmetry element and cannot be removed by external strains.
elements.id-string-35: Thus, even when the system is strain-tuned to a point where the in-plane lattice parameters are equivalent ($a=c$), the system does not possess a 4-fold rotational symmetry, and hence can never be truly tetragonal.
elements.id-string-36: The consequences of strain-tuning become more interesting when considering its effect on ErTe$_3$'s charge density wave (CDW) state.
elements.id-string-37: RTe$_3$ crystals host a unidirectional, incommensurate CDW.
elements.id-string-38: For un-strained ErTe$_3$, this onsets via a continuous phase transition at a critical temperature $T_{CDW}$ = 268K, with the wavevector oriented along the $c$-axis.\cite{Ru2006}\cite{Ru_th} The instability is apparently driven, at least in large part, by a strongly q-dependent electron-phonon coupling, and softening of the associated phonon mode which has been observed via inelastic x-ray scattering \cite{Maschek2015} \cite{Maschek2018}.
elements.id-string-39: The structural motifs that make up the building blocks of RTe$_3$ result in a near-equivalence of the electronic structure and phonon spectrum in the two inequivalent in-plane directions.
elements.id-string-40: This near-equivalence is reflected in a substantial softening of the phonon mode at the CDW wavevector in the transverse ($a$-axis) direction, even while the phonon in the $c$-axis direction approaches zero energy as $T \to T_{CDW}$.

elements.id-string-155: In closing, we comment on some wider implications of our observations.
elements.id-string-156: First, having established that modest strains can rotate the direction of the CDW in ErTe$_3$, we note that domain formation is to be anticipated whenever a crystal of RTe$_3$ is held under some conditions that fix the lateral dimensions, at least as long as the spontaneous strain that develops at T$_{CDW}$ is greater than the strain that is caused by fixing the sample dimensions.
elements.id-string-157: In particular, one should anticipate domain formation whenever thin samples are bonded to a platform.
elements.id-string-158: Since this is a standard geometry for many experiments, consideration of domain formation should be included in interpretation of a variety of experimental results.

elements.id-string-161: Second, while the symmetry element that renders ErTe$_3$ orthorhombic for all values of externally induced strains is a glide plane, other structural motifs, for example the 1d chains in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-\delta}$, can play a similar role.

elements.id-string-176: Appendix A: Measurement of Strains in the Experiment
elements.id-string-177: \begin{figure} \includegraphics[scale=1]{appendix_a.jpg} \caption{ Displacement measured from strain gauge on platform as a function of displacement measured from capacitive sensor shown in blue. At low strains, this function is linear (dashed black line). The strain gauge reading starts to deviate substantially from the capacitive reading at ~7um.} \end{figure}
elements.id-string-178: In this experimental set-up, a uniaxial stress is applied to the sample platform producing strains $\Delta L_x/L_x$, $\Delta L_y/L_y$, and $\Delta L_z/L_z$ in the platform.
elements.id-string-179: $L_x$ is the effective or active length of the platform which, for a similar shape 'bowtie' has been determined by simulation to be 3.47mm.\cite{Park2020} The capacitive sensor in the strain cell allows for measurement of the displacement between the cell's jaws.
elements.id-string-180: For low strains we approximate that this displacement is entirely transmitted to the active (narrow) region of the 'bowtie' platform, giving a measurement of $\Delta L_x$.
elements.id-string-181: (In practice though, this transmission is likely between 80-90$\%$.) Once the titanium  plastically deforms, however, (at approximately 0.2$\%$), the transmission of the cell's displacement to the platform falls off significantly, such that the capacitive reading is no longer an accurate determination of $\Delta L_x$.
elements.id-string-182: Instead for large displacements, $\Delta L_x$ can be determined by mounting a strain gauge directly onto the Ti platform and a corrective function can be developed to convert the capacitance reading to the actual strain.\ref{figa} This correction is the primary origin of the error bars shown in Fig. 4(a), for example.
elements.id-string-183: While we report our data in terms of measured platform strain, this is a reasonable approximation for the macroscopic strain experienced by the ErTe$3$ sample.
elements.id-string-184: Simulations of samples studied reveal that close to 90$\%$ of the platform strain $\Delta L_x/L_x$ is transmitted to the sample.
elements.id-string-185: This transmission can also be verified by direct measurement of the sample lattice parameters with XRD.
elements.id-string-186: The width of our samples was chosen such that the transverse strain $\Delta L_z/L_z$ is set by the Poisson ratio of the platform rather than the sample.
elements.id-string-187: The sample will experience additional strains however due to differential thermal contraction between it and the platform.
elements.id-string-188: Since RTe$_3$ contracts 5 times faster than titanium, the sample will experience additional tensile strains as it cools.
elements.id-string-189: The sample's macroscopic strain is differentiated from its microscopic strain in the CDW state, as discussed in the main text.
elements.id-string-190: Above the CDW state, $\epsilon_{xx}$ and $\Delta L_x/L_x$ are equivalent.
elements.id-string-191: This changes with the presence of domains.
elements.id-string-192: While the dimensions of the sample change when the platform is strained, within a single domain $\epsilon_{xx}$ is zero and will not become nonzero until the sample is strained into one of the monodomain states.
elements.id-string-193: This can be seen clearly in the Fig. 2b where there is no change in the lattice parameter in the mixed domain phase.

elements.id-string-205: In Fig. \ref{figc}, the elastoresistivity data are replotted using (1) a smooth function to model $T_{CDW}$ as a function of $(\Delta L_x/L_x)$, as also done in Figure 4(c), (this is the most accurate method, appropriate even far from the bicritical point); (2) using two straight lines to model $T_{CDW}$ as a function of $(\Delta L_x/L_x)$ (this method is less accurate over the entire strain range, but presumably is still a good description close to the bicritical point); and (3) fixing $T_{CDW}$ as a constant (this is clearly unphysical, but is included to demonstrate how robust the result is).
elements.id-string-206: Comparing Figures 7(a) and 7(b), it can be seen that although the exact shape of the peak in the elastoresistance changes  depending on the values of $T_{CDW}$ as a function of $(\Delta L_x/L_x)$, nevertheless the peak feature is robust.
elements.id-string-207: If $T_{CDW}$ is assumed to be constant (Figure 7(c)), the peak feature is less pronounced, because the elastoresistivity response grows rapidly at high strains due to the strong enhancement of $T_{CDW}$ which is here neglected.
elements.id-string-208: Nevertheless, a peak in the elastoresistivity is still observed close to $T_{CDW}$ even in this case.
